sections.h2: Where is the Iredell County Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
Iredell County runs two Register of Deeds offices, one in Statesville and one in Mooresville, and both are open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. according to the county staff directory.

  • Statesville: 211 Constitution Ln, Statesville, NC 28677, phone 704-872-7468
  • Mooresville: 610 E Center Ave, Mooresville, NC 28115, phone 704-663-4533
  • Fax for the office: 704-878-5426

Beyond deeds, the office issues certified birth and death records, marriage licenses and military discharge copies, and it administers notary oaths. Anyone can see the records, since the office says all of its information is public except military discharges.

A seller in Iredell County mostly meets this office through the closing attorney, who sends the deed and deed of trust for recording. The office is the place to confirm that a deed reached the record and in what order it was filed.

sections.h2: What does the Register of Deeds do in a home sale?
sections.html:
It records the deed that moves title from the seller to the buyer and the deed of trust that secures the buyer's loan, then indexes both by the names of the parties. State law gives the recorded document its priority.

Under G.S. 47-18, a conveyance is not valid against lien creditors or purchasers for value until it is registered in the county where the land lies, and priority follows the order of registration. That is why closings end with recording rather than with the signing.

The Iredell office also sets out the limits of what its staff can do. State law bars the office from preparing deeds or helping to prepare them, and from searching titles or giving title opinions. Adding or removing a name from a deed means a new deed drafted, notarized and recorded in the county where the property is located, so most owners hire an attorney.

Judgments and liens are filed with the Clerk of Superior Court, not with the Register of Deeds. The Iredell FAQ explains that a judgment is valid for ten years, can be extended another ten, and becomes a lien on land you own or acquire in that period. Ask a closing attorney to check for any judgment before a sale.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a deed in Iredell County?
sections.html:
A standard deed costs $26 for the first 15 pages and $4 for each page after that, and a deed of trust is $64 for the first 35 pages plus $4 per extra page. These are statewide fees set by G.S. 161-10, and the Iredell FAQ confirms the $26 and $4 figures for separation papers.

Recording fees that apply in Iredell County under G.S. 161-10
ItemFee as printed
Instrument, first 15 pages$26.00
Each additional page$4.00
Deed of trust or mortgage, first 35 pages$64.00
Satisfaction or cancellation of a deed of trustNo fee
Plat, per sheet$21.00
Certified copy, first page$5.00
Nonstandard document add-on$25.00

Source: North Carolina General Statutes, G.S. 161-10. The statute calls these fees complete and exclusive, and they are collected before filing.

Iredell also lists its own copy prices. A copy of a recorded deed is $.25 per page, and a printed copy of a recorded property map is $1.00. Ask the office for the current fee list before you mail anything, since mailing a copy back to you carries its own charge.

sections.h2: Who pays the Iredell County deed transfer tax?
sections.html:
The seller, called the transferor in the statute, pays the excise tax to the Register of Deeds before the deed can be recorded. The rate is $1 for each $500 of value, rounded up for any part of $500.

The state excise tax statute splits the money, with one half going to the county general fund and the other half remitted to the Department of Revenue. The Iredell FAQ answers a common question this way: excise tax applies to all conveyances of real property in the state, and its own example is that a $2,000 purchase of land owes $4.00 at recording.

The tax is figured on the consideration or value of the interest conveyed. The statute puts the duty on the seller, so look for this line on the closing statement and ask your attorney how your contract treats it.

sections.h2: How do I search Iredell County land records?
sections.html:
Use the online record search linked from the county Register of Deeds page. Iredell says it has land records from December 1788 forward, and that it indexes documents by the names of the parties as the law requires.

The county's Land Records page offers a guide to searching, plus separate guides for indexing rules and for finding land before 1964. The Register's page also describes deeds, deeds of trust, plat maps and powers of attorney that go back to the 1700s.

The county's online terms say the records site is in testing while the office moves from one software vendor to another. They warn that the information can be inaccurate or incomplete and is not an official source of record, so rely on a certified copy from the office for anything that matters to a sale.

  • Searching by owner: the tax office GIS maps show who owns a parcel, and the tax staff can help at 704-878-3020.
  • Paid-off mortgage: the lender sends a certificate of satisfaction for recording, and the office can email or mail you a copy.
  • Lost deed: the office will provide a copy at $.25 per page if you give names and a year.

sections.h2: Does the Register of Deeds collect property tax in Iredell County?
sections.html:
No. Property tax is billed and collected by Iredell County Tax Administration in Statesville, and the Register of Deeds only records documents. The two offices still meet at a sale, because the buyer's attorney wants the tax account current.

The collector says it will take payment at closing if you ask, and will accept a prepayment based on the previous year's rate when the new bill is not yet out. The county tax rate is 0.50 per $100 for 2026, per the county rates page, and towns such as Statesville and Mooresville add their own. Real estate taxes are due September 1, and the county reports interest of 2 percent beginning January 6.

Ownership for tax purposes is set on January 1. A seller who closes later in the year remains liable for that year's bill unless the contract shifts it, so check the proration line on the settlement statement.

sections.h2: What does Iredell County look like by the numbers?
sections.html:
Iredell County had an estimated 211,798 residents on July 1, 2025, per Census QuickFacts, and it covers 574.41 square miles of land with about 93,711 housing units.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 2024: 71.9 percent
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $321,400
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $1,714
  • Median household income: $81,419
  • Median gross rent: $1,252
  • Building permits in 2025: 1,835

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Iredell County?
faqs.a: You record it at the Register of Deeds in Statesville (211 Constitution Ln) or Mooresville (610 E Center Ave). Both offices are open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

faqs.q: How much is the recording fee for a deed in Iredell County?
faqs.a: A standard instrument costs $26 for the first 15 pages and $4 for each additional page. A deed of trust costs $64 for the first 35 pages, plus $4 per added page.

faqs.q: Who pays the excise tax on a deed in Iredell County?
faqs.a: The seller pays it before recording, at $1 per $500 of value. Your contract and closing statement show how it is handled.

faqs.q: Can the Iredell County Register of Deeds write my deed?
faqs.a: No. State law bars the office from preparing deeds or helping prepare them. Hire a North Carolina attorney, then bring the signed and notarized deed in for recording.

faqs.q: Where do I find a judgment against my property in Iredell County?
faqs.a: Judgments are filed with the Clerk of Superior Court at 704-832-6600, not with the Register of Deeds. A judgment lasts ten years and can be extended for another ten.
